---
title: "How this book is organized"
---

::: {.callout-warning .review-pending title="Under development"}
This chapter is part of a book in active development and has not yet
been through the author's review. Content may change as the review
advances.
:::

This book is built as **twelve studios**. A studio is a stretch of real
research work with a product at the end: an artifact you make, date, and
version, from your first working agreement to the public release of a
finished project. Each studio opens with a page that says what you will
produce, then hands you its **lessons** — short readings that each settle one
research decision and end with an **It is your turn** section — and then
brings you back to produce the studio's artifact. Read, do, return. By the
last studio you have not read about a research project; you have one.

Studio 1 hands you the operating rules for everything that follows: the
principle (AI is your arm and your research assistant, not your brain), your
role (research director), the protocol you run every time you delegate
(SDIIVDD), and the ownership that never transfers (your name on the claim).

![Studio 1 hands you the operating rules; Studios 2–12 are the road they
carry you down.](../images/part1_arc.png){fig-alt="Diagram. Inside a large
Studio 1 frame, four lessons chain left to right: the principle, your role,
the protocol, the ownership. An arrow leads down to a row of five boxes
grouping Studios 2 through 12, from framing the question to releasing the
finished project."}

The road has a shape worth naming. Studios 2–4 turn curiosity into a
declared, diagnosable research design. Studios 5–6 develop your pathway —
observational or experimental, descriptive, causal, or predictive — and put
your data and measurement under governance. Studios 7–8 produce your first
reproducible analysis and then try to break it. Studios 9–10 write your
claims down with their boundaries and adapt them to whatever venue will
test them. Studios 11–12 make the work reproducible by strangers and hand
the next cycle its agenda. Six arcs, twelve studios, one project.

Two more things, so the structure never surprises you. First, not every
lesson is for every reader at every moment: pathway lessons serve the
pathway you declared, and a few lessons are optional overlays — each one
says so at its **It is your turn** section, and skimming what does not
serve your project is using the book correctly. Second, every studio's
artifact is a **versioned checkpoint**, not a box you tick: when later
evidence changes your mind, you write the next version and say why. That
record of changes is part of the research, not an admission of failure.
